title: New Open-Source Context Specs Released
publisher: Capital One Tech; Rico Romero, Komal Pandamaneti and Marseld Dedgjonaj
summary: Capital One describes a planning, validation and implementation workflow that stores specifications on disk, supplies context per implementation slice, and composes reusable domain experts with verification signals. The article presents its own framework and experience rather than a controlled comparison.
supports: Curate task-specific context and preserve handoff artifacts.
Keep domain knowledge reusable across a workflow.
Separate planning, specialized review and implementation responsibilities.
limitations: Article body accessible without bypassing a paywall. Framework self-report; reviewer agreement does not establish correctness. Corroboration: https://github.com/capitalone/context-specs and https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents . Current repository behavior may differ from this publication snapshot.

title: I Replaced My SDLC with AI Agents — Here’s the Framework That Actually Worked
summary: A project retrospective describes requirements, architecture, coding, critique and knowledge roles connected by Markdown artifacts and shell orchestration. It distinguishes structural validation from content review, records decisions between phases, and limits revision attempts before human escalation.
supports: Define role inputs, outputs and bounded handoffs.
Use deterministic checks alongside semantic review.
Preserve assumptions and architecture decisions between sessions.
limitations: Article body accessible; single-project self-report, not an independently reproduced evaluation. Reported productivity and coverage numbers are not adopted. General workflow patterns are corroborated by https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents ; the article's automation commands were neither downloaded nor executed.

title: The New Engineering Stack: Specs, Context, and Agents
summary: The author argues that explicit intent, nonfunctional constraints, persistent context and verification should guide AI-assisted work. Specifications and repository instructions are presented as complementary artifacts that help engineers keep agent execution aligned with design intent.
supports: Capture nonfunctional expectations before implementation.
Maintain concise repository context and a durable specification.
Teach engineers to review intent and constraints.
limitations: Article body accessible; opinion and experience do not establish universal productivity improvements. Context-management concepts are corroborated by https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents . Instruction files and MCP alone are not security boundaries; enforcement requires separately configured tools and permissions.

title: Agentic Development Best Practices
summary: The author proposes versioned governance, limited autonomy, documented reasons for rules, evidence retention, and human ownership of consequential decisions. He distinguishes reviewing program behavior from checking that a change complied with organizational constraints.
supports: Record the policy version used for a run.
Set action permissions according to impact.
Make human accountability and policy-change ownership explicit.
limitations: Article body accessible; practitioner governance proposal, not a compliance standard. Passing tests do not prove overall correctness. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/218/final corroborates integrating secure development practices into an SDLC, not this author's specific gates or universal approval policy.

title: Testing the Testers: How to Validate AI-Generated Automation Scripts
summary: The author warns that generated tests can pass while checking weak assertions or unrealistic inputs. He proposes reviewing test intent, negative cases, boundaries and representative data, and using mutation testing to investigate whether tests detect altered behavior.
supports: Review generated tests as production artifacts.
Trace assertions to requirements and realistic failure cases.
Use mutation testing selectively to assess test sensitivity.
limitations: Article body accessible; anecdotal numerical results are not generalizable and are omitted. Mutation-testing mechanics are corroborated by https://stryker-mutator.io/docs/ . Mutation scores complement other evidence and do not prove completeness or justify arbitrary universal thresholds.

title: Shifting Observability Left in the SDLC
summary: This practitioner article argues for instrumenting applications during development and using telemetry during deployment and troubleshooting. It discusses OpenTelemetry as a way to standardize instrumentation independently of a particular observability vendor.
supports: Include instrumentation requirements during design and implementation.
Connect development feedback to deployment and operational evidence.
Separate telemetry interfaces from backend selection.
limitations: Article body accessible; vendor-associated publication with promotional links, and not specifically an AI-agent delivery study. https://opentelemetry.io/docs/what-is-opentelemetry/ corroborates the telemetry and vendor-neutrality concepts. Claimed delivery improvements were not independently measured.

title: Comparing 15 Spec-Driven Development Frameworks, Artifacts, and Decision Paths— SDD
summary: The visible introduction frames framework selection around differing process rigor and installed artifacts. It advertises a broader comparison, but the matrix and substantive decision paths are behind a member-only boundary and were not evaluated.
supports: Framework rigor and artifact burden are useful comparison questions.
This entry is a discovery lead, not evidence for framework rankings.
limitations: Member-only story: only title, date and introductory material accessible; no paywall bypass. Star counts, rankings and unseen matrix claims are excluded. https://github.com/github/spec-kit independently documents one framework's current workflow; it does not validate the unavailable comparison.
